glance: NSK and NTN signed the binding deal to merge into NSK-NTN Ltd. in October 2027, and an Anthropic mathematician claimed a Claude-assisted proof of the Riemann Hypothesis that has yet to be checked. Intuit sold Mailchimp for a third of what it paid, ChatGPT and Google Search both moved further toward agent-style interfaces, and Anthropic's shares fell on their second day. In automotive, Germany saw its first full-day metal strikes in eight years, the US moved closer to a legal ban on Chinese-linked cars, and two new papers show how to make lubrication and clutch simulations faster and better correlated.
brief: This is Vertical News for Saturday the twenty-first of November. Japan's NSK and NTN signed their binding merger agreement on Friday. They will form a holding company called NSK-NTN, listing in Tokyo on the first of October 2027, and they are aiming for fifty to sixty billion yen in savings. Carmakers buying from both should expect fewer product lines. In AI, Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge claimed a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, worked out with Claude over forty-one days and released as machine-checkable code. Hours later, a Stanford researcher posted a rival proof made without AI. Neither has been peer reviewed, so treat both as unconfirmed. Intuit is selling Mailchimp to Bending Spoons for three point six eight billion dollars, about a third of what it paid, saying AI inside QuickBooks will do the job. OpenAI is testing a ChatGPT app built around personal agents, though not in Europe, and Google's homepage now has a sidebar of AI Mode threads. Anthropic's shares fell eight and a half percent on their second day. In Germany, a hundred and fifty-one thousand metal workers held the first full-day strikes in eight years. US lawmakers are close to a law banning Chinese-linked cars, with a likely exemption for Mercedes. Cheap EU-built electric cars from Volkswagen and Renault reached UK order books, but the EU–UK summit did not fix rules of origin. Ford Trucks is preparing for the battery passport, and GM will score suppliers on automation. Finally, two new papers speed up lubrication simulation and correlate clutch models with test data.

stories.headline: NSK and NTN sign the definitive deal to merge into NSK-NTN Ltd. from 1 October 2027
stories.why: Two of the world's largest bearing makers become one owner of hub, transmission and EV motor bearings, which changes sourcing for OEMs and Tier 1s.
body: NSK and NTN signed a binding business integration agreement on Friday, approved by both boards the same day, six months after their May memorandum of understanding. A joint share transfer will create a holding company, NSK-NTN Ltd., that owns both. Each NSK share becomes one share in the new company and each NTN share becomes 0.353, with about 709 million new shares issued. Shareholders vote on 25 June 2027, both companies delist on 29 September and the holding company lists in Tokyo on 1 October 2027. Foreign competition approvals are still needed.

NSK's Akitoshi Ichii will be CEO and NTN's Eiichi Ukai co-CEO, with an NTN-nominated non-executive chair of a ten-member board and head offices in both Tokyo and Osaka. The target is 50–60 billion yen of operating profit synergies by the year to March 2031: about 40% from purchasing and logistics, 30% from production sites, 20% from admin and R&D and 10% from sales. Combined sales last financial year were about 1.74 trillion yen.

European car and truck makers that dual-source between the two should expect product-line and plant consolidation and new commercial terms. Together with SKF's Vertevo spin-off on 1 December, the automotive bearing supplier map is being redrawn within a year.

stories.headline: Anthropic mathematician claims a Claude-assisted proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, and a rival human proof appears hours later
stories.why: If it holds, it would be the strongest sign yet that AI plus formal verification can solve problems experts could not, but nothing is confirmed.
body: Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic, posted a short note on Friday claiming a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis and its generalised form, open since 1859. He says he worked it out with Claude over 41 days, from 6 October to 16 November. The proof was released only as Lean code, a formal language that a computer can check, split into a 14-part archive. Alpöge says a full natural-language version would run past 250,000 pages and has promised a readable explanation. He said he chose the timing himself, a day after Anthropic's stock market debut, and rejected links to the share price.

Hours later, Stanford's Ravi Vakil, president of the American Mathematical Society, posted a draft proof of the generalised hypothesis by Stanford postdoc Alessandro Masullo, which he described as made without AI. Early checks say Alpöge's Lean statement does match the hypothesis, but there is no peer review, and Anthropic and the Clay Institute had not commented.

Treat this as unconfirmed. For engineers, the interesting part is the method: machine-checked proofs let people trust output they cannot read line by line, the same idea behind formal verification in chip and software sign-off.

stories.headline: Intuit sells Mailchimp to Bending Spoons for $3.68 billion, a third of what it paid, betting on AI inside QuickBooks
stories.why: A big SaaS product is being replaced by AI features in a suite, and AI search is hurting how products find customers.
body: Milan-based Bending Spoons, owner of Evernote, Vimeo, Eventbrite and Airtable, is buying Mailchimp from Intuit at an enterprise value of 3.68 billion dollars. Intuit gets 3.31 billion in cash and puts 368 million into new Bending Spoons shares. The deal was announced after the US market closed on Thursday and is expected to close in early 2027. Intuit paid about 12 billion dollars for Mailchimp in 2021; Mailchimp revenue fell 1% to 313 million dollars last quarter.

Chief executive Sasan Goodarzi said AI built into QuickBooks can serve small firms' lead-to-cash needs better than owning a separate marketing tool. CFO Sandeep Aujla said people now turn to AI for the first answer, which weakens how Credit Karma gets customers from search. Intuit cut its revenue guidance for fiscal 2027 and its shares fell about 10–13% after hours.

For product strategists, two lessons stand out: point products are being folded into AI features of larger platforms, and acquisition through search is no longer reliable when users ask an assistant first.

stories.headline: OpenAI tests a redesigned ChatGPT app built around personal agents, but not in the EU or UK
stories.why: The chat box is turning into app-style navigation around an always-on agent, a pattern other assistants are likely to follow.
body: OpenAI has started testing a new mobile layout for ChatGPT, shown in a demo by OpenAI's Thibault Sottiaux. A bottom tab bar has three parts: Home, with a greeting and an 'Ask anything' field; a dedicated tab for the user's 'dot', an always-on personal agent marked as an early preview; and a grid of tools including Projects, Images, Scheduled, Codex, Plugins, Finance, Health and Sites. Users can press and hold a tool to pin it to the tab bar.

The design is switched on in Settings. The first wave covers adult Pro users plus a small group of Plus users, and dots are also coming to US Business Standard customers. The European Economic Area, the UK, Switzerland and South Korea are excluded for now, so most of our readers will not see it yet.

For designers, the shift is from one conversation to a home screen with a persistent agent and pinnable tools. It raises familiar questions about discoverability and how much a personal agent should surface on its own. It is a test, not a general release.

stories.headline: Google's desktop homepage gets a sidebar of AI Mode threads, rolling out worldwide
stories.why: The world's most-used search page now treats a query as an ongoing conversation, which changes how people arrive at websites and products.
body: Google is gradually adding a collapsible left-hand sidebar to google.com on desktop, worldwide, as announced by Search vice president Robby Stein. A thin grey rail opens into a panel with options for a new thread, a list of search threads, a Notes area where users can add a Gemini notebook, and recent AI Mode conversations that reopen where they left off. The logo and search box stay in the centre.

Stein said people's questions are rarely one-off, and that the sidebar made a big difference in testing. Google has not said whether mobile will get it or whether users can turn it off. AI Mode reached one billion monthly users in May, according to Google.

Digital Trends notes that Search now looks a lot like a chatbot app. For product and marketing teams, more journeys will start and continue inside Google's AI threads rather than on a list of links, so being cited inside answers matters more than ranking alone.

stories.headline: Anthropic shares fall 8.5% on day two as the greenshoe lifts IPO proceeds to about $93.5 billion
stories.why: The second day shows how quickly sentiment around AI listings can swing, with knock-on effects for AI pricing and spending.
body: After closing its first day at 97.17 dollars, Anthropic's stock fell more than 10% before the market opened on Friday, traded around 86 dollars at midday and closed at 88.91 dollars, down 8.5% and only slightly above the 83-dollar IPO price. Coverage pointed to a broad tech sell-off, turmoil at Nvidia and uncertainty around the midterms.

Underwriters exercised their full option to sell 147 million extra shares, about 12.2 billion dollars at the IPO price. That takes IPO proceeds to about 93.5 billion dollars, or roughly 119.5 billion including the earlier 26 billion private placement. The filing showed a third-quarter operating loss of 567 million dollars, partly due to about five billion dollars of compute costs. Bloomberg reports that the stock could join the Nasdaq 100 as soon as December.
For teams that build on Claude, day-to-day share moves change little. The more important thing is that Anthropic now reports publicly, so pricing, capacity and spending will be watched every quarter.

stories.headline: IG Metall's first 24-hour strikes in eight years hit 151,000 workers at more than 100 companies
stories.why: Production gaps at German OEMs and suppliers are now a real risk for early 2027 planning.
body: IG Metall says 151,000 employees at more than 100 companies stopped work for a full day on Friday, with some stoppages starting on Thursday night shifts. TRT World reported action at BMW and Audi plants in Bavaria, suppliers in Baden-Württemberg and shipyards in the north. About 464,000 people had already joined shorter warning strikes since the peace obligation ended on 31 October.

The third bargaining round failed earlier in November. The union wants 5% more pay over 12 months, profit-sharing and binding commitments on jobs and sites. Employers have offered a one-off payment of 1% of annual pay in July 2027, which struggling firms could withhold, and a permanent 1.3% rise from July 2028, over 26 months. The agreement covers about 3.7 million workers. No fourth round has been scheduled and more action is planned for next week.
This is the industry-wide round, separate from Volkswagen's in-house talks that start on 24 November. Suppliers, including drivetrain and bearing plants, should expect more disruption before a deal.

stories.headline: US Congress nears a law banning Chinese-linked cars, with a likely way out for Mercedes-Benz
stories.why: A law would lock in the US split for any carmaker or supplier with Chinese owners, including Geely-linked Swedish brands.
body: Bloomberg reports, citing unnamed sources, that lawmakers are close to a deal in the post-election session to write a ban on Chinese-linked cars into law, and want it on President Trump's desk before January. A bill from Senators Bernie Moreno and Elissa Slotkin would bar carmakers with more than 15% Chinese ownership from selling connected cars in the US.

That would catch Mercedes-Benz, where BAIC holds 9.98% and Geely founder Li Shufu 9.69%. Revised wording shown to carmakers on Wednesday would allow passive stakes without voting rights, and Alabama Senator Katie Britt expects Mercedes to be protected. Geely-controlled Polestar has already stopped US sales after it did not receive a Commerce Department waiver, even for the US-built Polestar 3.

Commerce rules already block Chinese-linked connected cars from model year 2027. A law would be far harder to reverse and would set fixed compliance demands on software and connectivity suppliers. It is not law yet.

stories.headline: Cheap EU-built EVs reach the UK as the EU–UK summit leaves EV rules of origin unresolved
stories.why: Small electric cars at combustion-car prices depend on cross-Channel trade terms that tighten on 1 January.
body: Volkswagen opened UK orders for the ID. Cross, a 4.15-metre compact SUV on the MEB+ platform built in Navarra, Spain. The 52 kWh versions cost £30,260 and £33,675, with up to 264 miles of WLTP range and a £1,500 grant; 37 kWh versions from £26,985 can be ordered from January. Renault priced the Slovenian-built Twingo E-Tech from £14,745 after the full £3,750 grant, with a 27.5 kWh LFP battery, a 60 kW motor and up to 163 miles of range. Orders open early in 2027.

On the same day, the EU–UK summit in Brussels agreed a common area for food and plant rules, a link between the two carbon markets targeted for 2028 and a youth mobility scheme. None of the reports we read mentioned a fix for the stricter EV and battery rules of origin due on 1 January 2027. Car industry groups SMMT and ACEA warned this week that fewer than one in four electrified cars and vans traded next year would comply, with a 10% tariff on the rest.
For product planners, both cars show where European volume is heading, and how much their UK business cases depend on a trade fix.

stories.headline: Ford Trucks hires Circulor to get its electric trucks ready for the EU battery passport
stories.why: From 18 February 2027 every EV traction battery sold in the EU needs a digital passport, and supplier data is the hard part.
body: Ford Otosan, the Ford and Koç Holding joint venture that sells under the Ford Trucks brand, is working with UK traceability firm Circulor to prepare its F-Line E electric trucks for the EU Battery Regulation. The work starts by mapping the battery supply chain from supplier data: companies, production sites and where materials come from. Higher-risk materials may need extra evidence and independent audits. Each battery will get a QR code linking to its passport data.

The F-Line E comes as a 19-tonne version with a 294 kWh NMC battery and up to 250 km of range, and a 26-tonne version with 392 kWh and up to 300 km. Circulor built the battery passport for the Volvo EX90 in 2024 and says it now traces materials for more than 1.4 million vehicles.

With under three months to go, carmakers and suppliers need the data model, supplier onboarding and audit trail in place. It is as much a product data and systems problem as a compliance task, and a natural fit for teams that already run PLM and traceability tools.

stories.headline: GM targets 20% more robots and automation in North American plants by 2028 and scores suppliers on it
stories.why: Automation plans are becoming a sourcing criterion, which affects how suppliers bid for OEM work.
body: General Motors aims to raise the use of robots and automation in its North American factories by 20% by 2028, citing rising manufacturing costs. It is building its own robots at its Kokomo, Indiana plant, mainly autonomous mobile robots that move parts and materials, and will keep buying equipment from outside suppliers. Its in-house robotics team had about 100 roboticists, AI engineers and hardware specialists last year.

Suppliers bidding for new GM contracts must now submit automation plans, which GM will grade on a scorecard that may count in contract awards. GM estimates its 2023 union agreement adds about 575 dollars of labour cost per vehicle. A UAW vice president criticised the push as a way to cut jobs; the next contract talks are in 2028.
For suppliers, including European ones serving US plants, this means automation roadmaps, simulation of cells and lines, and data on uptime may become part of quotations, not only price and quality.

stories.headline: Neural-network starting guesses cut CPU time for EHL simulations by about 60%
stories.why: Faster lubrication solvers make it cheaper to run the many contact cases needed for gear and bearing design and virtual validation.
stories.source: Lubricants (MDPI) · Leibniz University Hannover · TU Munich (FZG)
body: A peer-reviewed paper in Lubricants by researchers from Leibniz University Hannover, TU Munich's gear research centre FZG, Arts et Métiers in Paris and the Lebanese American University uses a small neural network to give a finite-element elastohydrodynamic lubrication solver a better place to start. The network, with two hidden layers of 32 neurons, was trained on almost 48,000 FEM runs of smooth line contacts and predicts pressure and film thickness at 101 points in under a millisecond.

Across 58 operating conditions, starting from the network's pressure prediction cut the median number of solver iterations by about 55% and CPU time by about 61%, compared with a standard Hertzian start with constant film thickness. Adding the predicted film thickness gave the smallest starting error but smaller savings, about 58% less CPU time. The solver still converges to the full physics answer, so accuracy is not traded away.

This is a practical way to use ML in simulation: speed up a trusted solver rather than replace it. The study covers smooth, isothermal line contacts, so extending it to point contacts, heat and roughness is the next test.

stories.headline: Test-corrected FE model and reduced-order surrogate predict wet clutch temperatures
stories.why: It is a clear example of correcting simulation with measurements before building a fast surrogate, a core step in virtual validation.
stories.source: Lubricants (MDPI) · Beijing Information Science & Technology University · CERTH / NTUA
body: Researchers from Beijing Information Science and Technology University, with partners at CERTH and the National Technical University of Athens, built an Abaqus model of a wet clutch friction pair, a copper-based disc against a steel disc. They corrected it using 12 thermocouple measurements, spreading the difference between measured and simulated temperatures over the field. A reduced-order model then compresses the corrected fields to 64 modes and maps pressure, speed and sliding time to the full temperature field. The paper is peer-reviewed.

Correcting against test data cut the model's error by almost half, from 3.5 to 1.8 °C mean absolute error. On held-out test cases the surrogate reached an R² of 0.956 and a mean error of 3.3 °C. Peak temperatures were less accurate, with errors above 100 °C in four cases, which the authors put down to measurement fluctuations.

For drivetrain teams, the workflow of correlate first, then reduce is directly transferable to clutches, brakes and bearings. The weak peak predictions show why surrogates still need checking where the limits are set.

watch.title: SKF Vertevo listing on 1 December
watch.text: The record date for the Vertevo share distribution is 27 November, and trading in SKF's automotive spin-off starts on 1 December, weeks after NSK and NTN agreed to merge.

watch.title: German metal strikes and VW talks
watch.text: IG Metall plans more action next week with no new bargaining round set, and Volkswagen's in-house pay talks open in Emden on 24 November.

watch.title: Checking the Riemann claims
watch.text: Mathematicians are checking the Lean code behind the Claude-assisted proof and reading the rival human draft. A readable version of the AI-assisted proof has been promised but not published.
